notes.front: What is Product Value, as Scrum.org describes it?
notes.back: The benefit a product gives its customers, and what the organization gains from it, in money or benefit to society.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org links it to things such as customer satisfaction and loyalty, brand reputation and how long a business lasts.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Value”, “What is Product Value?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: A library’s e-book app: readers borrow books without travelling, and the council meets its literacy aims at lower cost.

notes.front: What is Evidence-Based Management (EBM)?
notes.back: A framework that helps people, teams and organizations make better-informed decisions toward their goals, using intentional experimentation and feedback.
notes.explanation: Complex problems have no easy solutions, so the Guide has organizations reach large goals in small, checked steps.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Definition of Evidence-Based Management”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Evidence-Based Management (EBM) is a framework that helps people, teams, and organizations make better-informed decisions to help them achieve their goals by using intentional experimentation and feedback.
notes.example: Like a gardener trying a new fertiliser on one bed and comparing the harvest before using it everywhere, applied to an organization’s decisions.

notes.front: In EBM, what is a Strategic Goal?
notes.back: An important thing the organization feels it needs to achieve to realize its Mission and Vision.
notes.explanation: It is aspirational and the path to it is uncertain, so the organization needs a series of practical targets on the way.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Strategic Goals, important things that the organization feels it needs to achieve to realize its Mission and Vision.
notes.example: A water charity aiming for every village in a region to have safe drinking water.

notes.front: In EBM, what is an Intermediate Goal?
notes.back: A goal whose achievement will indicate that the organization is on the path to a Strategic Goal.
notes.explanation: A Strategic Goal is aspirational with an uncertain path, so the organization needs practical targets like this one on the way.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Intermediate Goals, achievements of which will indicate that the organization is on the path to a Strategic Goal.
notes.example: For the water charity: a first district where every village has a working well.

notes.front: In EBM, what is an Immediate Tactical Goal?
notes.back: The current focus of the organization’s improvement efforts.
notes.explanation: It is the nearest of the three goal levels, the one experiments are aimed at right now.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Immediate Tactical Goals, which are the current focus of the organization’s improvement efforts.
notes.example: For the water charity: cutting the time to repair a broken pump this quarter.

notes.front: In EBM’s categories of measures, what are outputs?
notes.back: Things the organization produces, such as product releases (including features), reports, defect reports and product reviews.
notes.explanation: The Guide warns that more outputs do not necessarily lead to better customer experiences.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Outputs. These are things that the organization produces, such as product releases (including features), reports, defect reports, product reviews, and so on.
notes.example: A bakery counting how many new cake recipes it put on the menu this month.

notes.front: In EBM, what are outcomes?
notes.back: Desirable things a customer or user of a product experiences: a new or improved capability they could not achieve before.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s examples are being able to travel somewhere faster, or to earn or save more money, than before.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Outcomes. These are desirable things that a customer or user of a product experiences. They represent some new or improved capability that the customer or user was not able to achieve before.
notes.example: A farmer who can now check crop prices by phone before market day, which she could not do before.

notes.front: In EBM, what are impacts?
notes.back: Results the organization or its non-customer stakeholders achieve when customers or users achieve their desired outcomes.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s examples are increased revenue or profit, improved market share and a higher share price.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Impacts. Results that the organization or its non-customer stakeholders (such as investors) achieve when customers or users of a product achieve their desired outcomes.
notes.example: A bus company’s rising ticket income after passengers find the new routes get them to work faster.

notes.front: In EBM, what is a hypothesis?
notes.back: A belief that doing something will lead to something else, such as delivering feature X will lead to outcome Y.
notes.explanation: Beliefs about what is valuable are merely assumptions until customers validate them, which is where hypotheses help.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A hypothesis is a belief that doing something will lead to something else, such as delivering feature X will lead to outcome Y.
notes.example: “If we let shoppers save a basket for later, fewer of them will abandon their order.”

notes.front: In EBM, what is an experiment?
notes.back: A test designed to prove or reject some hypothesis.
notes.explanation: Organizations measure the results of experiments as evidence of progress toward their goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: An experiment is a test that is designed to prove or reject some hypothesis.
notes.example: Offering the save-for-later button to half of the shop’s visitors for two weeks and comparing abandoned orders.

notes.front: In EBM, what is the Experiment Loop?
notes.back: The cycle that moves an organization from its Current State toward its goals in small, measured steps (experiments) using explicit hypotheses.
notes.explanation: It leads first to the Immediate Tactical Goal, then the Intermediate Goal, and ultimately the Strategic Goal.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Experiment Loop (shown in Figure 1) helps organizations move from their Current State toward their Immediate Tactical Goal, their Intermediate Goal, and ultimately their Strategic Goal, by taking small, measured steps, called experiments, using explicit hypotheses.
notes.example: Like a cook tasting and adjusting a sauce in small steps, but with the goal and the test written down first.

notes.front: In EBM, what is a Key Value Area (KVA)?
notes.back: One of a set of perspectives on value and on the organization’s ability to deliver value.
notes.explanation: Each one is a lens on a different aspect of either value or the ability to deliver it, which keeps the view balanced.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: EBM provides a set of perspectives on value and the organization’s ability to deliver value. These perspectives are called Key Value Areas (KVAs).
notes.example: Like the separate gauges on a car’s dashboard, each showing a different aspect of how the trip is going.

notes.front: Which KVA is Current Value (CV)?
notes.back: The KVA whose measures quantify the value that the product delivers today.
notes.explanation: It considers only what exists right now, not value that might exist in the future.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Current Value (CV) Measures that quantify the value that the product delivers today
notes.example: For a train company: how satisfied passengers, staff and shareholders are with the service running this month.

notes.front: Which KVA is Unrealized Value (UV)?
notes.back: The KVA whose measures quantify the potential future value that could be realized if the organization met the needs of all potential customers or users.
notes.explanation: Looking at it helps an organization maximize the value it realizes from a product or service over time.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Unrealized Value (UV) Measures that quantify the potential future value that could be realized if the organization met the needs of all potential customers or users
notes.example: For the train company: the commuters who still drive because no train reaches their town.

notes.front: Which KVA is Ability to Innovate (A2I)?
notes.back: The KVA whose measures quantify the effectiveness of an organization in delivering new capabilities.
notes.explanation: Looking at it aims to maximize the organization’s ability to deliver new capabilities and innovative solutions.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Ability to Innovate (A2I) Measures that quantify the effectiveness of an organization in delivering new capabilities
notes.example: For the train company: how much of its engineers’ time goes into new services rather than patching old timetabling software.

notes.front: Which KVA is Time-to-Market (T2M)?
notes.back: The KVA whose measures quantify how quickly the organization can deliver, and learn from the feedback it gathers from experiments.
notes.explanation: Looking at it aims to minimize the time it takes to deliver something potentially valuable.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Time-to-Market (T2M) Measures that quantify how quickly the organization can deliver and learn from feedback they gather from experiments
notes.example: For the train company: how many days pass between an idea for a new ticket type and passengers being able to buy it.

notes.front: In EBM, what is a Key Value Measure (KVM)?
notes.back: A measure that helps an organization understand its current state, desired future state, or what influences its ability to improve.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s appendix lists example KVMs for each KVA, as illustrations rather than requirements.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: KVMs listed below are presented to show the kinds of measures that might help an organization to understand its current state, desired future state, and factors that influence its ability to improve.
notes.example: Like choosing which readings to take for a patient: body temperature is one measure, chosen because it says something about their state.

notes.front: What is technical debt, as the EBM Guide defines it?
notes.back: The extra development and testing work that arises when “quick and dirty” solutions lead to later remediation.
notes.explanation: The Guide says it harms the delivery of value and adds avoidable waste and risk; it lists it as an A2I measure.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: A concept in programming that reflects the extra development and testing work that arises when “quick and dirty” solutions result in later remediation.
notes.example: Hard-coding a tax rate to meet a deadline, then having to find and fix every copy of it when the rate changes.

notes.front: According to Scrum.org, what is the only way a Scrum Team delivers product value?
notes.back: By releasing an Increment of the product.
notes.explanation: Work that is Done but not yet in users’ hands has not delivered its value yet.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Value”, “What is Product Value?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Scrum Team produces a Done Increment every Sprint but holds them all back for one big launch in nine months. In Scrum.org’s view, when does this work start delivering product value?
notes.back: B) Only once an Increment is released.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org treats releasing an Increment as the only route by which a Scrum Team delivers product value.
notes.choices:
A) Each Sprint, when the Increment meets the Definition of Done
B) Only once an Increment is released
C) When the Product Owner accepts the work
notes.choicesExplained: A and C describe work being finished or accepted; on Scrum.org’s account, value reaches people only through a release.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Value”, “What is Product Value?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Scrum.org says organizations must keep checking, by measurement, that their products are valuable. What are they producing if they do not?
notes.back: Waste.
notes.explanation: Monitoring product value is what lets them manage a product, a portfolio and a business strategy well.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Value”, “What is Product Value?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A leadership team sets next year’s product investments by the most confident opinion in the room, and never checks the results. Which EBM idea is missing?
notes.back: C) Better-informed decisions through intentional experimentation and feedback.
notes.explanation: EBM exists to help people make better-informed decisions toward goals by experimenting and using feedback.
notes.choices:
A) A fixed budget for each team
B) A longer planning horizon
C) Better-informed decisions through intentional experimentation and feedback
notes.choicesExplained: A and B change how the plan is made, not whether the decisions are tested against evidence.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Definition of Evidence-Based Management”, p. 2
notes.evidence: helps people, teams, and organizations make better-informed decisions to help them achieve their goals by using intentional experimentation and feedback.

notes.front: If an organization implements only parts of EBM, is the result Evidence-Based Management?
notes.back: No. Implementing parts of it is possible, but the result is not Evidence-Based Management.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide’s End Note says this in the same way the Scrum Guide says it of Scrum.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “End Note”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Although implementing only parts of EBM is possible, the result is not Evidence-Based Management.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, which way of expressing purpose states the change the organization wants to make in the world?
notes.back: A Vision Statement.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists it with the Mission Statement and goals as ways organizations create purpose and alignment.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A Vision Statement, an expression of the change that the organization wants to make in the world.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, which statement expresses why the organization is uniquely capable of achieving its Vision?
notes.back: A Mission Statement.
notes.explanation: Organizations exist to achieve something they think they, uniquely, can achieve; the Mission Statement says why.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A Mission Statement, an expression of why the organization is uniquely capable of achieving the Vision Statement.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, what do goals add to a Mission and Vision?
notes.back: Concrete progress: without goals, the Mission and Vision are simply lofty aspirations.
notes.explanation: Goals sit on several levels and timescales, and without a Mission and Vision they lack a compelling purpose.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Organizations form goals to make concrete progress toward achieving their Mission and Vision. Without goals, the Mission and Vision are simply lofty aspirations.

notes.front: Why must an organization use empiricism to reach a Strategic Goal?
notes.back: Because such goals are so big and far away, with many uncertainties along the journey.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls forming hypotheses, running experiments and measuring the results “empiricism in action with EBM”.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: These goals are so big and far away, with many uncertainties along the journey that the organization must use empiricism to achieve them.

notes.front: What is a Strategic Goal usually focused on?
notes.back: Achieving a highly desirable but unrealized outcome for a specific group of people.
notes.explanation: The Guide keeps the hedge “usually”; achieving it improves the recipients’ happiness, safety, security or well-being.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Strategic Goal is usually focused on achieving a highly desirable but unrealized outcome for a specific group of people.

notes.front: How certain is the path to an Intermediate Goal?
notes.back: Often still somewhat uncertain, but not completely unknown.
notes.explanation: It is a practical target on the way to an aspirational Strategic Goal, whose own path is uncertain.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: The path to the Intermediate Goal is often still somewhat uncertain, but not completely unknown.

notes.front: How do organizations move toward their Immediate Tactical Goals?
notes.back: They form hypotheses about improvements, which become the basis of experiments they run.
notes.explanation: They measure the results (evidence) to judge progress and to choose next steps, which may include adjusting goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: organizations form hypotheses about improvements they can make to move toward their Immediate Tactical Goals. These hypotheses form the basis of experiments that they run to try to improve.

notes.front: A city library service sets: “Every resident can borrow any book they want within a day.” Which EBM goal level is this most likely to be?
notes.back: A) Strategic Goal.
notes.explanation: It is big, far away and full of uncertainty, and it describes the effect wanted for residents rather than a means.
notes.choices:
A) Strategic Goal
B) Intermediate Goal
C) Immediate Tactical Goal
notes.choicesExplained: B would be a milestone showing the library is on the path; C would be the narrow thing the team is improving right now.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: These goals are so big and far away, with many uncertainties along the journey that the organization must use empiricism to achieve them.

notes.front: The same library service sets: “A next-day delivery pilot succeeds in one district.” Which EBM goal level is this most likely to be?
notes.back: B) Intermediate Goal.
notes.explanation: Achieving it would indicate the service is on the path to its Strategic Goal, and the path to it is uncertain but not unknown.
notes.choices:
A) Strategic Goal
B) Intermediate Goal
C) Immediate Tactical Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A is the far-off aim the pilot serves. C is narrower: the current focus of improvement work.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Intermediate Goals, achievements of which will indicate that the organization is on the path to a Strategic Goal.

notes.front: The same library service sets: “This month, cut the time to find a reserved book on the shelves.” Which EBM goal level is this most likely to be?
notes.back: C) Immediate Tactical Goal.
notes.explanation: It is the current focus of improvement efforts, the target that today’s experiments aim at.
notes.choices:
A) Strategic Goal
B) Intermediate Goal
C) Immediate Tactical Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are further away and less certain; this is a near-term target for current work.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Immediate Tactical Goals, which are the current focus of the organization’s improvement efforts.

notes.front: Why should an organization’s measurable goals, measures and experiments be made transparent?
notes.back: To encourage organizational alignment.
notes.explanation: The Guide first requires goals to be measurable, so that the organization can tell whether each is achieved.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: These measurable goals, measures, and experiments should be made transparent in order to encourage organizational alignment.

notes.front: Should a Strategic Goal name the effect the organization wants, or the means of getting there?
notes.back: The effect; an activity needed to reach it may be necessary, but it is not the Strategic Goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s illustration measures a goal by the people affected, not by an activity count.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: the goal is focused on the effects of the disease, and not on the means for achieving the desired impact.

notes.front: In EBM, what are inputs, and does more input mean more value for customers?
notes.back: Things the organization spends money on; there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value customers experience.
notes.explanation: Inputs are still necessary, and they can set constraints on experiments, such as a spending limit.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience.

notes.front: In EBM’s categories of measures, what are activities?
notes.back: Things people in the organization do, such as working, attending meetings, writing code or creating reports.
notes.explanation: The Guide notes that activities, like outputs, are easy to measure, unlike outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Activities. These are things that people in the organization do, such as perform work, go to meetings, have discussions, write code, create reports, attend conferences, and so forth.

notes.front: A hospital’s technology team tracks “money spent on cloud hosting this quarter”. Which EBM category of measure is this?
notes.back: A) Input.
notes.explanation: It is money the organization spends, which EBM places among inputs.
notes.choices:
A) Input
B) Activity
C) Output
D) Outcome
E) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: Inputs are money spent; activities are what people do; outputs are what is produced; outcomes are what customers experience; impacts are what the organization gains.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on.

notes.front: The same technology team tracks “hours spent in planning meetings”. Which EBM category of measure is this?
notes.back: B) Activity.
notes.explanation: Going to meetings is something people in the organization do, so EBM counts it as an activity.
notes.choices:
A) Input
B) Activity
C) Output
D) Outcome
E) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: Inputs are money spent; activities are what people do; outputs are what is produced; outcomes are what customers experience; impacts are what the organization gains.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Activities. These are things that people in the organization do, such as perform work, go to meetings, have discussions

notes.front: The same technology team tracks “number of app versions shipped”. Which EBM category of measure is this?
notes.back: C) Output.
notes.explanation: Releases are things the organization produces, which EBM calls outputs.
notes.choices:
A) Input
B) Activity
C) Output
D) Outcome
E) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: Inputs are money spent; activities are what people do; outputs are what is produced; outcomes are what customers experience; impacts are what the organization gains.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Outputs. These are things that the organization produces, such as product releases (including features)

notes.front: The same technology team tracks “patients can now book a scan in two minutes instead of twenty”. Which EBM category of measure is this?
notes.back: D) Outcome.
notes.explanation: It is a new or improved capability the users experience, which EBM calls an outcome.
notes.choices:
A) Input
B) Activity
C) Output
D) Outcome
E) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: Inputs are money spent; activities are what people do; outputs are what is produced; outcomes are what customers experience; impacts are what the organization gains.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: They represent some new or improved capability that the customer or user was not able to achieve before.

notes.front: The hospital group tracks “income from private patients rose 8%”. Which EBM category of measure is this?
notes.back: E) Impact.
notes.explanation: It is a result the organization achieves when users achieve their outcomes, which EBM calls an impact.
notes.choices:
A) Input
B) Activity
C) Output
D) Outcome
E) Impact
notes.choicesExplained: Inputs are money spent; activities are what people do; outputs are what is produced; outcomes are what customers experience; impacts are what the organization gains.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Examples include things like increased revenue or profit, improved market share, and increased share price.

notes.front: Can an outcome be negative in EBM?
notes.back: Yes: when the value a customer or user experiences declines, for example when a service they relied on is no longer available.
notes.explanation: Outcomes are defined by what customers experience, so a loss counts just as a gain does.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: can also be negative, as in the case where the value a customer or user experiences declines from previous experiences, for example when a service they previously relied upon is no longer available.

notes.front: Which measures does the EBM Guide call easy to measure, and which difficult?
notes.back: Activities and outputs are easy; outcomes are difficult.
notes.explanation: This is the problem most organizations face: they may gather lots of data with too little information about their ability to deliver value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The problem most organizations face, which is often reflected in the things they measure, is that measuring activities and outputs is easy, while measuring outcomes is difficult.

notes.front: A team celebrates shipping 40 features this quarter, all through overtime. Customer satisfaction has not moved. What does the EBM Guide say about this?
notes.back: A) More hours and more features do not necessarily lead to improved customer outcomes.
notes.explanation: Hours are activities and features are outputs; the Guide separates both from the outcomes customers experience.
notes.choices:
A) More hours and more features do not necessarily lead to improved customer outcomes
B) Satisfaction will follow automatically once enough features ship
C) The team should measure hours more precisely
notes.choicesExplained: B assumes outputs guarantee outcomes, which the Guide denies. C measures activity more closely, but that still says nothing about outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: For example, working more hours (activities) and delivering more features (outputs) does not necessarily lead to improved customer experiences (outcomes).

notes.front: When are positive impacts sustainably achievable, according to the EBM Guide?
notes.back: Only when customers experience improved outcomes.
notes.explanation: Impacts are what the organization gains when customers achieve their desired outcomes, so they rest on those outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Positive Impacts are only sustainably achievable when customers experience improved outcomes.

notes.front: What usually happens when an organization improves impacts without improving customer outcomes?
notes.back: It usually harms the organization.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s cases are cutting quality to raise profit, and selling below cost to gain revenue and market share at the expense of profitability.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While it is possible for organizations to improve impacts without improving customer outcomes, doing so usually harms the organization

notes.front: To lift this year’s profit, a kettle maker switches to cheaper parts, and more kettles now fail. Profit rises. How does the EBM Guide view this?
notes.back: C) An impact gained without better customer outcomes, which usually harms the organization.
notes.explanation: The Guide says impacts must be achieved in a sustainable way that does not harm the organization’s long-term viability.
notes.choices:
A) A good result, because profit is the impact that matters
B) An improved outcome, because profit rose
C) An impact gained without better customer outcomes, which usually harms the organization
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that the gain came from worse outcomes for customers. B confuses an impact (profit) with an outcome (what customers experience).
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Achieving impacts is important, but they have to be achieved in a sustainable way that does not harm the organization’s long-term viability.

notes.front: What is the first step in the journey toward a Strategic Goal?
notes.back: Understanding your Current State.
notes.explanation: You need to know what customers experience now and how fast you can improve it before you can set realistic short and medium term goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The first step in the journey toward a Strategic Goal is understanding your Current State to frame your thinking about where and how you need to improve.

notes.front: What is the first step of the Experiment Loop?
notes.back: Forming a hypothesis for improvement, and deciding how you will know, by measurement, whether the experiment succeeded.
notes.explanation: The idea is drawn from experience and aimed at the Immediate Tactical Goal.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Forming a hypothesis for improvement. Based on experience, form an idea of something you think will help you move toward your Immediate Tactical Goal, and decide how you will know whether this experiment succeeded based on measurement.

image.alt: A cycle of four boxes joined by arrows: 1. Form a hypothesis (an idea to move toward the Immediate Tactical Goal); 2. Run the experiment (make the change, gather data); 3. Inspect results (did the measures improve?); 4. Adapt (goals or approach, from what you learned), leading back to step 1.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, pp. 6–7

notes.front: In the Experiment Loop, what does running the experiment involve?
notes.back: Making the change you think will help, and gathering data to support or refute your hypothesis.
notes.explanation: The data gathered here is what the next step, inspecting results, relies on.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Running your experiments. Make the change you think will help you to improve, and gather data to support or refute your hypothesis.

notes.front: In the Experiment Loop, what question does inspecting your results answer?
notes.back: Did the change improve results, based on the measurements made?
notes.explanation: The Guide warns that not all changes improve things; some make things worse.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Inspecting your results. Did the change you made improve your results based on the measurements you have made? Not all changes do; some changes actually make things worse.

notes.front: In the Experiment Loop’s last step, what may be adapted?
notes.back: Your goals or your approach, based on what you learned.
notes.explanation: Goals can change because of outside events, and the tactics to reach them may need revising.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Adapting your goals or your approach based on what you learned. Both your goals and your improvement experiments will likely evolve as you learn more about customers, competitors, and your organization's capabilities.

notes.front: A team changed its sign-up form two weeks ago and has collected sign-up data every day since. Which Experiment Loop step comes next?
notes.back: B) Inspecting the results against the measures it chose.
notes.explanation: After running an experiment and gathering data, the loop inspects whether the change improved results before adapting.
notes.choices:
A) Forming a new hypothesis straight away
B) Inspecting the results against the measures it chose
C) Adapting the Strategic Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A skips learning from the data just gathered. C comes after inspection, and adapting may not even be needed if the change worked.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Inspecting your results. Did the change you made improve your results based on the measurements you have made?

notes.front: Is failing to reach an Immediate Tactical Goal, because an experiment did not give the expected results, a bad thing?
notes.back: No. What you learned helps you devise new experiments that may yield better results.
notes.explanation: Not all changes improve results; the Guide treats what is learned as the basis for the next experiments.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: This is not a bad thing, and what you learned helps you to devise new experiments that may yield better results.

notes.front: The Experiment Loop is a variation on which earlier cycle?
notes.back: The Shewhart Cycle, popularized by W. Edwards Deming, also called the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle.
notes.explanation: The Guide notes this lineage in a footnote to its description of the loop.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Experiment Loop is a variation on the Shewhart Cycle, popularized by W. Edwards Deming, also sometimes called the PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle

notes.front: According to the EBM Guide, what does every feature and every requirement really represent?
notes.back: A hypothesis about value.
notes.explanation: Customers may not share the company’s opinion of a feature’s value; beliefs about value are merely assumptions until customers validate them.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Every feature and every requirement really represents a hypothesis about value.

notes.front: Must a whole feature be built to find out whether it is valuable?
notes.back: Not necessarily: it may be enough to build just enough to validate the critical assumptions.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “may be sufficient”, so a partial build is an option to weigh, not a rule.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: A sponsor is certain that a loyalty-points scheme will make customers shop more often, and wants the whole scheme built. How would EBM treat the idea?
notes.back: A) As a hypothesis about value, tested by an experiment that may need only part of the scheme.
notes.explanation: Every feature is a hypothesis about value, and building enough to validate critical assumptions may be sufficient.
notes.choices:
A) As a hypothesis about value, tested by an experiment that may need only part of the scheme
B) As a known requirement, since the sponsor is certain
C) As an output target: the scheme counts as value once shipped
notes.choicesExplained: B treats a belief as validated before customers have confirmed it. C mistakes an output for value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: One of the goals of an empirical approach is to make these hypotheses explicit and to consciously design experiments that explicitly test the value of the features and requirements.

notes.front: What does an organization risk if it cannot keep making progress toward its long-term goals (Unrealized Value)?
notes.back: Succumbing to stagnation and complacency.
notes.explanation: The Guide wants all four KVAs watched: value today, responding to change, sustaining innovation and progress toward long-term goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: And they must be able to continually make progress toward their long-term goals (Unrealized Value) or they risk succumbing to stagnation and complacency.

notes.front: In the 2024 EBM Guide, in what terms may the organizational capability KVAs (A2I and T2M) be measured?
notes.back: Either outcomes or outputs.
notes.explanation: They reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes, rather than those outcomes themselves.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes, and so may be measured in terms of either outcomes or outputs.

notes.front: Is Time-to-Market a market value KVA or an organizational capability KVA?
notes.back: An organizational capability KVA.
notes.explanation: The 2024 Guide groups T2M with A2I as capability KVAs; CV and UV are the market value KVAs.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Market value KVAs (UV, CV) reflect customer outcomes. Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes

notes.front: Does Current Value consider value that might exist in the future?
notes.back: No; it considers only what exists right now.
notes.explanation: Future potential is the job of Unrealized Value; CV is about value delivered to customers and stakeholders at the present time.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: it considers only what exists right now, not the value that might exist in the future.

notes.front: Which CV question concerns the people who use or buy the product?
notes.back: How happy are users and customers today, and is their happiness improving or declining?
notes.explanation: It is the first of the three CV questions, which organizations need to keep re-evaluating.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: How happy are users and customers today? Is their happiness improving or declining?

notes.front: Which CV question concerns the people who produce the value?
notes.back: How happy are your employees today, and is their happiness improving or declining?
notes.explanation: The Guide calls employees the producers of value; happy employees are more engaged and productive.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: How happy are your employees today? Is their happiness improving or declining?

notes.front: Which CV question concerns those who fund the organization?
notes.back: How happy are your investors and other stakeholders today, and is it improving or declining?
notes.explanation: Profit is one way the Guide suggests of measuring investor happiness.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: How happy are your investors and other stakeholders today? Is their happiness improving or declining?

notes.front: The only ferry to an island earns record profit, yet passenger surveys are poor. What does the EBM Guide suggest about judging its Current Value?
notes.back: B) Look at CV from several perspectives; profit can be high while customer satisfaction is low when customers have few alternatives.
notes.explanation: Profit shows investor happiness and economic impact, while customer happiness shows where to improve to keep customers.
notes.choices:
A) Profit is enough: record profit means high Current Value
B) Look at CV from several perspectives; profit can be high while customer satisfaction is low when customers have few alternatives
C) Only employee happiness matters for CV
notes.choicesExplained: A relies on one perspective. C drops the customer and investor perspectives, which the Guide keeps alongside employees.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: If your customers have few alternatives to your product, you may have high profit even though customer satisfaction is low. Considering CV from several perspectives will give you a better understanding of your challenges and opportunities.

notes.front: When customers experience a gap between their current experience and the one they would like, what does that gap represent in EBM?
notes.back: An opportunity, which is measured by Unrealized Value.
notes.explanation: The Guide also calls this the satisfaction gap between a beneficiary’s desired outcome and their current experience.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: When customers, users, or clients experience a gap between their current experience and the experience that they would like to have, the difference between the two represents an opportunity; this opportunity is measured by Unrealized Value.

notes.front: What are Strategic Goals formed from, in terms of UV and CV?
notes.back: Some satisfaction gap, and an opportunity to decrease UV by increasing CV.
notes.explanation: In EBM, a Strategic Goal usually targets a desirable but unrealized outcome, which is what Unrealized Value names.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Strategic Goals are formed from some satisfaction gap and an opportunity for an organization to decrease UV by increasing CV.

notes.front: What does considering both CV and UV give an organization?
notes.back: A way to balance present and possible future benefits.
notes.explanation: CV covers only what exists now and UV covers potential value, so together they span both.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The consideration of both CV and UV provides organizations with a way to balance present and possible future benefits.

notes.front: A start-up’s tutoring app has few paying users so far, but surveys show a huge unmet demand from parents. How would EBM read its CV and UV?
notes.back: A) Low CV, high UV: investing to raise CV is probably warranted.
notes.explanation: The Guide says a product with low CV but very high UV shows great market potential, so investment is probably justified.
notes.choices:
A) Low CV, high UV: investing to raise CV is probably warranted
B) High CV, low UV: stop investing
C) Low CV means the product has no value worth pursuing
notes.choicesExplained: B misreads both: few users means low CV, and unmet demand means high UV. C ignores UV, the potential future value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Investing in the product to try to boost CV is probably warranted, given the potential returns, even though the product is not currently producing high CV.

notes.front: A spreadsheet tool has led its market for 20 years; customers are very satisfied and there are no close rivals. How would EBM read its CV and UV?
notes.back: C) High CV, low UV: it may not warrant much new investment.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes such a very profitable product near the end of its investment cycle as a classic cash cow.
notes.choices:
A) Low CV, high UV: invest heavily
B) High CV, high UV: double the team
C) High CV, low UV: it may not warrant much new investment
notes.choicesExplained: A and B assume large untapped opportunity; satisfied customers and no rivals point to little UV left.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Conversely, a product with very high CV, large market share, no near competitors, and very satisfied customers may not warrant much new investment

notes.front: What two questions does the EBM Guide use to re-evaluate A2I?
notes.back: What prevents the organization from delivering new value? What prevents customers or users from benefiting from that innovation?
notes.explanation: The first looks inside the organization; the second looks at the customer’s side of innovation.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: What prevents the organization from delivering new value? 2. What prevents customers or users from benefiting from that innovation?

notes.front: What happens to an organization’s capacity to innovate as low-value features and systemic impediments accumulate?
notes.back: It falls, because more budget and time go into maintaining the product or overcoming impediments.
notes.explanation: Anything that stops customers benefiting from innovation, such as hard-to-install new versions, reduces A2I too.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: As low-value features and systemic impediments accumulate, more budget and time are consumed maintaining the product or overcoming impediments, reducing its available capacity to innovate.

notes.front: A team spends most of each Sprint fixing defects in old code and supporting four versions of its product. Which KVA does the EBM Guide say this weakens?
notes.back: B) Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: Remedying poor quality and maintaining multiple product variations are among the Guide’s examples of what impedes delivering new capabilities.
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Ability to Innovate
C) Unrealized Value
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are market value KVAs about customer outcomes; the drain described is on the organization’s capability to deliver new value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: spending too much time remedying poor product quality, needing to maintain multiple variations of a product due to lack of operational excellence

notes.front: What are two questions the EBM Guide asks to evaluate T2M?
notes.back: Any two of: how fast can it learn from new experiments, adapt, or test new ideas with customers?
notes.explanation: T2M looks at how quickly the organization can deliver and learn from feedback it gathers from experiments.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: How fast can the organization learn from new experiments and information? 2. How fast can you adapt based on the information? 3. How fast can you test new ideas with customers?

notes.front: Improving T2M improves the frequency of what?
notes.back: How often the organization can potentially change Current Value.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that the result must be measured to know whether customers’ value actually improved.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Improving T2M helps improve the frequency at which an organization can potentially change CV.

notes.front: What change to a product release does the EBM Guide say can dramatically improve T2M?
notes.back: Reducing the number of features in the release.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this with a floor: the release must still improve value for some customers or users.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Reducing the number of features in a product release can dramatically improve T2M

notes.front: What is the smallest release possible, according to the EBM Guide?
notes.back: One that delivers at least some incremental improvement in value to some subset of the product’s customers or users.
notes.explanation: Many organizations also remove non value-added activities from development and delivery to improve T2M.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: the smallest release possible is one that delivers at least some incremental improvement in value to some subset of the customers/users of the product.

notes.front: A Product Owner plans one release of twelve features every six months and wants to learn faster from customers. Which EBM suggestion fits?
notes.back: A) Release fewer features at a time, each release still improving value for some users.
notes.explanation: Reducing features per release can dramatically improve T2M, as long as each release still adds some value for some users.
notes.choices:
A) Release fewer features at a time, each release still improving value for some users
B) Add more features to each release so customers see more at once
C) Keep the plan and survey customers yearly
notes.choicesExplained: B lengthens the wait for feedback. C leaves the time to learn unchanged.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Time-to-Market (T2M)”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Reducing the number of features in a product release can dramatically improve T2M; the smallest release possible is one that delivers at least some incremental improvement in value

notes.front: What should Immediate Tactical Goals do to Current Value and Unrealized Value?
notes.back: Improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.
notes.explanation: Even goals aimed at effectiveness or feedback speed should keep customer satisfaction in sight through CV and UV.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Immediate Tactical Goals should improve Current Value and reduce Unrealized Value.

notes.front: What happens when an organization targets improvements only in A2I and T2M without monitoring CV and UV?
notes.back: It is focused only on internal processes that may not help satisfy customers or achieve value.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that this can lead to, or indicate, a lack of outcome-based goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: When an organization targets improvements only in A2I and T2M without monitoring CV and UV, they are focused only on internal processes that may not help them further satisfy customers or achieve value.

notes.front: A department halves its deployment time and celebrates, but nobody has checked whether customers are any better off. What does the EBM Guide warn about?
notes.back: C) Improving T2M without monitoring CV and UV focuses only on internal processes.
notes.explanation: Faster delivery is a capability gain; CV and UV show whether customers actually benefit.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: faster deployment always raises value
B) The department should now measure A2I instead
C) Improving T2M without monitoring CV and UV focuses only on internal processes
notes.choicesExplained: A assumes a capability gain reaches customers. B swaps one capability KVA for another and still ignores CV and UV.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: This can lead to, or be an indication of, a lack of outcome-based goals.

notes.front: Does EBM prescribe specific Key Value Measures?
notes.back: No. To encourage adaptability, EBM defines no specific KVMs; the appendix lists examples.
notes.explanation: The examples show the kinds of measures that might help; each organization picks what fits its situation.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: To encourage adaptability, EBM defines no specific Key Value Measures (KVMs).

notes.front: A consultant tells a Product Owner that EBM “requires” Revenue per Employee and Release Frequency on every dashboard. Is that right?
notes.back: B) No; EBM defines no specific KVMs, and those are examples to choose from.
notes.explanation: The Guide leaves measures open to encourage adaptability.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; the appendix is mandatory
B) No; EBM defines no specific KVMs, and those are examples to choose from
C) Yes, but only for Scrum Teams
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat the appendix as requirements; the Guide presents it as examples.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 14
notes.evidence: To encourage adaptability, EBM defines no specific Key Value Measures (KVMs). KVMs listed below are presented to show the kinds of measures that might help

notes.front: Which example CV measure is the ratio of gross revenue to number of employees?
notes.back: Revenue per Employee.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a key competitive indicator within an industry, and it varies significantly by industry.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Current Value (CV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: The ratio (gross revenue / # of employees) is a key competitive indicator within an industry.

notes.front: Which example CV measure compares the product’s total expenses and costs, including operational costs, with revenue?
notes.back: Product Cost Ratio.
notes.explanation: It shows what the product costs to run relative to what it brings in.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Current Value (CV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Total expenses and costs for the product(s)/system(s) being measured, including operational costs compared to revenue.

notes.front: Which example CV measure uses sentiment analysis to gauge employee engagement, energy and enthusiasm?
notes.back: Employee Satisfaction.
notes.explanation: It answers the CV question about how happy employees are today.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Current Value (CV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Some form of sentiment analysis to help gauge employee engagement, energy, and enthusiasm.

notes.front: Which example CV measure uses sentiment analysis to gauge customers’ engagement and happiness with the product?
notes.back: Customer Satisfaction.
notes.explanation: It answers the CV question about how happy users and customers are today.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Current Value (CV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Some form of sentiment analysis to help gauge customer engagement and happiness with the product.

notes.front: Which example CV measure tracks usage by feature, to infer how useful customers find the product?
notes.back: Customer Usage Index.
notes.explanation: It also shows whether actual usage meets expectations of how long users should take with a feature.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Current Value (CV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Measurement of usage, by feature, to help infer the degree to which customers find the product useful

notes.front: Which example UV measure estimates the share of the market the product might achieve if it better met customer needs?
notes.back: Potential Market Share.
notes.explanation: It measures value not yet realized, which is what UV is about.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Unrealized Value (UV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: the potential market share that the product might achieve if it better met customer needs.

notes.front: Which example UV measure is the difference between a customer’s desired experience and their current experience?
notes.back: Customer or User Satisfaction Gap.
notes.explanation: This gap is the opportunity that Unrealized Value measures.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Unrealized Value (UV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: The difference between a customer or user’s desired experience

notes.front: Which example UV measure indicates the experience the customer would like to have?
notes.back: Desired Customer Experience or satisfaction.
notes.explanation: It sits beside the satisfaction gap measure among the Guide’s UV examples.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Unrealized Value (UV) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: A measure that indicates the experience that the customer would

notes.front: Which example T2M measure counts integrated and tested builds per time period?
notes.back: Build and Integration Frequency.
notes.explanation: For a team releasing frequently or continuously, the Guide says actual release measures supersede it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 14
notes.evidence: The number of integrated and tested builds per time period.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure counts releases per time period, such as daily, weekly or quarterly?
notes.back: Release Frequency.
notes.explanation: It helps reflect the time needed to satisfy the customer with new and competitive products.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The number of releases per time period, e.g. continuously, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, etc.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the time spent correcting product problems between “ready to release” and the actual release?
notes.back: Release Stabilization Period.
notes.explanation: It helps represent the impact of poor development practices and the underlying design and code base.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The time spent correcting product problems between the point the

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the average time from detecting an error to fixing it?
notes.back: Mean Time to Repair.
notes.explanation: It helps reveal how efficiently an organization fixes errors.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The average amount of time it takes from when an error is detected and when it is fixed.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure runs from when work starts on a release until it is actually released?
notes.back: Customer Cycle Time.
notes.explanation: It helps reflect an organization’s ability to reach its customer.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The amount of time from when work starts on a release until the point where it is actually released.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure runs from when an idea is proposed, or a hypothesis formed, until a customer can benefit from it?
notes.back: Lead Time.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a contributing factor for customer satisfaction; it may vary by customer and product.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The amount of time from when an idea is proposed, or a hypothesis is formed until a customer can benefit from that idea.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the time from code being committed to it running successfully in production?
notes.back: Lead Time for Changes.
notes.explanation: Unlike Lead Time, it starts at committed code rather than at the idea.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The amount of time to go from code-committed to code successfully running in production.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure counts how often a new version of the product was deployed (released) to customers?
notes.back: Deployment Frequency.
notes.explanation: The Guide points to a 2019 industry report for more on it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The number of times that the organization deployed (released) a new version of the product to customers/users.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the time from the start of a service outage to full restoration?
notes.back: Time to Restore Service.
notes.explanation: Unlike Mean Time to Repair, it is about a whole service being available again.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The amount of time between the start of a service outage and the restoration of full availability of the service.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the total time to sketch an idea, build it, deliver it to users and learn from their usage?
notes.back: Time-to-Learn.
notes.explanation: It ends with learning from usage, not with delivery.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The total time needed to sketch an idea or improvement, build it, deliver it to users, and learn from their usage.

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the average time from when an impediment is raised until it is resolved?
notes.back: Time to remove Impediment.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a contributing factor to lead time and employee satisfaction.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The average amount of time from when an impediment is raised

notes.front: Which example T2M measure is the time between receiving feedback or new information and responding to it?
notes.back: Time to Pivot.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a measure of true business agility.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Time-to-Market (T2M) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: A measure of true business agility that presents the elapsed time between when an organization receives feedback or new information and when it responds to that feedback

notes.front: Which example A2I measure shows how far employees are aligned with, and bought into, the organization’s goals?
notes.back: Employee Engagement.
notes.explanation: It sits under A2I, while Employee Satisfaction sits under CV.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 15
notes.evidence: A measure of the degree to which employees are aligned with

notes.front: Which example A2I measure is the percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities?
notes.back: Innovation Rate.
notes.explanation: It gives insight into the organization’s capacity to deliver new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities, divided by total product effort or cost.

notes.front: Which example A2I measure tracks the change in defects since the last measurement?
notes.back: Defect Trends.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines a defect as anything that reduces the product’s value to a customer, user or the organization.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Measurement of change in defects since last measurement.

notes.front: Which example A2I measure is the percentage of time teams spend working on product and value?
notes.back: On-Product Index.
notes.explanation: It appears among the A2I examples, measures of effectiveness in delivering new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The percentage of time teams spend working on product and value.

notes.front: Which example A2I measure counts the versions of a product currently being supported?
notes.back: Installed Version Index.
notes.explanation: It reflects the effort spent supporting and maintaining older versions of software.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The number of versions of a product that are currently being supported.

notes.front: Which example A2I measure counts how often, in a period, the team was interrupted to fix a problem in an installed product?
notes.back: Production Incident Count.
notes.explanation: It can help indicate the product’s stability. The 2024 appendix still says “Development Team”; the 2020 Scrum Guide says Developers.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The number of times in a given period that the Development Team was

notes.front: Which example A2I measure counts the different versions (or variants) of a product or service?
notes.back: Active Product (Code) Branches.
notes.explanation: It gives insight into the potential impact of change and the resulting complexity of work.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The number of different versions (or variants) of a product or service.

notes.front: Which example A2I measure is the time spent applying changes across different versions of a product or service?
notes.back: Time Spent Merging Code Between Branches.
notes.explanation: Like counting branches, it gives insight into the impact of change and the complexity of work.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16

notes.front: Which example A2I measure covers time lost to interruptions, switching between tasks and helping people outside the team?
notes.back: Time Spent Context-Switching.
notes.explanation: The Guide says such examples give simple insight into the size of the problem.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: time spent switching between tasks, and time lost when team members are interrupted to help people outside the team

notes.front: Which example A2I measure is the percentage of released changes that degrade service and need remediation?
notes.back: Change Failure Rate.
notes.explanation: Remediation means work such as a hotfix, a rollback or a patch.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Ability to Innovate (A2I) KVM”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The percentage of released product changes that result in degraded service

notes.front: How do EBM’s three goal levels differ in distance and certainty?
notes.back: Strategic: far off and uncertain. Intermediate: on the path, somewhat uncertain. Immediate Tactical: the current focus of improvement.
notes.explanation: Organizations form hypotheses aimed at the Immediate Tactical Goal in order to progress toward the other two.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Because a Strategic Goal is aspirational and the path to achieving it is uncertain, the organization needs a series of practical targets, like Intermediate Goals.

image.alt: A rising staircase of four boxes joined by arrows: Current State (where you are today), then Immediate Tactical Goal (current focus of improvement efforts), then Intermediate Goal (shows you are on the path; path somewhat uncertain), then Strategic Goal at the top (aspirational; far away, with many uncertainties). A note says each step is reached by small, measured experiments and goals are adapted as you learn.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), Figure 1 and “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, pp. 3–4

notes.front: What is the difference between an output and an outcome in EBM?
notes.back: An output is something the organization produces; an outcome is something desirable the customer or user experiences.
notes.explanation: Measuring outputs is easy and measuring outcomes is difficult, yet outcomes are what organizations need to reach their goals.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: However, delivering valuable outcomes to customers is essential if organizations are to reach their goals.

notes.front: In the 2024 EBM Guide, what separates the market value KVAs from the organizational capability KVAs?
notes.back: Market value KVAs (CV, UV) reflect customer outcomes; capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes.
notes.explanation: Capability KVAs may therefore be measured as outcomes or outputs, while the market value KVAs stay tied to customer outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Uses Key Value Areas to Examine Improvement Opportunities”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Market value KVAs (UV, CV) reflect customer outcomes. Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization’s ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes

image.alt: Four boxes in two rows split by a dashed line. Top row, labelled “Market value: reflects customer outcomes”: Unrealized Value (UV), potential future value if all potential customers’ needs were met; Current Value (CV), value the product delivers today. Bottom row, labelled “Organizational capability: ability to deliver those outcomes”: Ability to Innovate (A2I), effectiveness in delivering new capabilities; Time-to-Market (T2M), how quickly it can deliver and learn from experiment feedback.
